```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set( collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", echo = FALSE,
                       message = FALSE, warning = FALSE,
                       fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4.5 )
```

```{r setup}
# summary tables are reused across sections
library( governance )
library( dplyr )
library( ggplot2 )

ov <- readRDS( "data/gov-overview.rds" )

blue  <- "#1696d2"
theme_set( theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
             theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
                   panel.grid.major.y = element_blank()) )

pct  <- function(x) paste0( round(100 * x), "%" )
num  <- function(x) format( x, big.mark = "," )

item_labels <- c(
  GI_REVIEW_AUDIT  = "Review or audit",
  GI_AUDIT         = "Audit",
  GI_AUDIT_CMTE    = "Audit committee",
  GI_ACCRUAL       = "Accrual accounting",
  GI_INDEP_MAJOR   = "Majority-independent board",
  GI_MINUTES_BOARD = "Board minutes",
  GI_MINUTES_CMTE  = "Committee minutes",
  GI_990_BOARD     = "990 given to board",
  GI_COI           = "Conflict-of-interest policy",
  GI_COI_DISCLOSE  = "Annual COI disclosure",
  GI_COI_MONITOR   = "COI policy monitored",
  GI_WHISTLE       = "Whistleblower policy",
  GI_RETENTION     = "Document retention policy",
  GI_COMP_CEO      = "CEO pay process",
  GI_COMP_OTH      = "Other-officer pay process",
  GI_990_WEB       = "990 on own website",
  RISK_INSIDER_BIZ = "Insider business transaction",
  RISK_LOAN        = "Loan to or from insider",
  RISK_FAM_TIES    = "Family or business ties",
  RISK_MGMT_CO     = "Management company",
  RISK_DIVERSION   = "Asset diversion"
)

pop23 <- ov$population[ ov$population$year == 2023, ]
sz    <- ov$scores_by_size
```

This article describes how governance practices vary across the U.S. nonprofit
sector. It covers every 501(c)(3) organization that e-filed a full Form 990 for
tax years 2021 to 2024: **`r num(pop23$n)` organizations in 2023**. Each was
scored with `get_features()` and `get_scores()`, so the results are on the
index scale described in `vignette("making-gov-scores")`. The scale is set so
that 2023 filers have mean 0 and standard deviation 1 on the underlying
(latent) governance factor; the estimated scores average
`r round(pop23$gov_mean, 2)` with a standard deviation of
`r round(pop23$gov_sd, 2)`, slightly less than 1 because each estimate is pulled
toward the mean in proportion to its uncertainty.

The figures come from summary tables built by
[`data-raw/make-overview-data.R`](https://github.com/Nonprofit-Open-Data-Collective/governance/blob/main/data-raw/make-overview-data.R)
and saved with the vignette; nothing is downloaded when the article is built.
Subsector and state come from the NCCS Business Master File; size is total
expenses (Form 990 Part I line 18).

## How common is each practice?

Practices range from nearly universal to rare. More than nine in ten filers
document board meetings, and most have a majority-independent board. About
two-thirds have a conflict-of-interest policy, about half have whistleblower and
retention policies or an independent review or audit, and fewer than one in ten
post their 990 on their own website.

```{r, fig.height = 5}
overall <- data.frame(
  item = names( ov$items_overall ),
  rate = unlist( ov$items_overall )
)
overall$kind  <- ifelse( grepl("^GI_", overall$item), "Practice", "Risk disclosure" )
overall$label <- item_labels[ overall$item ]

overall |>
  filter( kind == "Practice" ) |>
  ggplot( aes(x = rate, y = reorder(label, rate)) ) +
  geom_col( fill = blue, width = 0.7 ) +
  geom_text( aes(label = pct(rate)), hjust = -0.15, size = 3.2 ) +
  scale_x_continuous( labels = scales::percent, limits = c(0, 1.08),
                      expand = c(0, 0) ) +
  labs( x = "Share of 2023 filers reporting the practice", y = NULL )
```

The number of practices reported is bimodal. One group of organizations
reports three or four practices, mostly the near-universal ones such as board
minutes and an independent board; a larger group reports 13 to 15. Fewer than 3% report
all 16, because posting the 990 online is rare even among organizations that do
everything else.

```{r, fig.height = 3.5}
ggplot( ov$count_dist, aes(x = gov_count, y = N / sum(N)) ) +
  geom_col( fill = blue, width = 0.8 ) +
  scale_x_continuous( breaks = 0:16 ) +
  scale_y_continuous( labels = scales::percent ) +
  labs( x = "Practices reported (gov_count)", y = "Share of 2023 filers" )
```

```{r, fig.height = 3.5}
ggplot( ov$score_hist, aes(x = bin + 0.125, y = N / sum(N)) ) +
  geom_col( fill = blue, width = 0.23 ) +
  scale_y_continuous( labels = scales::percent ) +
  labs( x = "gov_score (bins of 0.25)", y = "Share of 2023 filers" )
```

The score distribution is lumpy, not bell-shaped, because the index is built
from 16 yes/no items: many organizations share the same response pattern and so
the same score. The tallest spike, just above −1.25, is organizations that
report only the near-universal practices, such as minutes and an independent
board. The cluster around 1.3 is organizations that report every practice except
posting the 990 online. Scores at the top and bottom are the least precise
(mean standard error about 0.6, against 0.2 in the middle).

## Size

Size is the strongest correlate of governance. The Spearman correlation between
`gov_score` and log expenses is **`r round(ov$cor_size$gov, 2)`**
(`r round(ov$cor_size$count, 2)` for the count). The average score rises by
`r round(sz$gov_mean[6] - sz$gov_mean[1], 1)` points from organizations spending
under \$100,000 to those spending \$40 million or more, and the typical
organization goes from about 6 practices to about 14.

```{r}
sz |>
  transmute( Size = size, Organizations = num(n),
             `Mean score` = round(gov_mean, 2),
             `25th pct` = round(gov_p25, 2), Median = round(gov_median, 2),
             `75th pct` = round(gov_p75, 2),
             `Mean practices` = round(count_mean, 1) ) |>
  knitr::kable( align = "lrrrrrr" )
```

```{r, fig.height = 3.5}
ggplot( sz, aes(y = size) ) +
  geom_linerange( aes(xmin = gov_p25, xmax = gov_p75), linewidth = 2,
                  colour = "#a2d4ec" ) +
  geom_point( aes(x = gov_median), colour = blue, size = 3 ) +
  scale_y_discrete( limits = rev ) +
  labs( x = "gov_score: median and interquartile range", y = "Total expenses" )
```

In the three largest size bands the 75th percentile is the same, 1.31: at least
a quarter of those organizations report every practice except posting the 990
online. The index has little room to separate organizations at the top.

Practices rise with size, but not equally. Audits show the steepest gradient,
from 12% of the smallest organizations to 98% of the largest; audits are often
required above state revenue thresholds and the federal single-audit
threshold. Written whistleblower and retention policies and the CEO pay process
rise almost as steeply. Board minutes are common at every size, and majority
independence *falls* slightly in the largest band, where the CEO often sits on
the board. The chart reads across: each row is a practice, each column a size
band.

```{r, fig.height = 6}
ib <- ov$items_by_size
ib <- ib[ grepl("^GI_", ib$item), ]
ib$label <- factor( item_labels[ as.character(ib$item) ],
                    levels = rev(item_labels[ names(ov$items_overall)[1:16] ]) )

ggplot( ib, aes(x = size, y = label, fill = rate) ) +
  geom_tile( colour = "white", linewidth = 1 ) +
  geom_text( aes(label = pct(rate), colour = rate > 0.6), size = 3 ) +
  scale_fill_gradient( low = "#e8f4fa", high = "#0a4c6a", limits = c(0, 1),
                       labels = scales::percent, name = NULL ) +
  scale_colour_manual( values = c(`TRUE` = "white", `FALSE` = "#1a1a1a"),
                       guide = "none" ) +
  labs( x = "Total expenses", y = NULL ) +
  theme( panel.grid = element_blank(), legend.position = "none" )
```

Because size drives adoption so strongly, the comparisons below are shown two
ways: the raw mean score, and a **size-adjusted** mean that compares each
organization with others in the same size band (the mean of `gov_score` minus
its size-band mean). A positive size-adjusted value means the group does better
than organizations of the same size elsewhere.

## Subsector

```{r}
sub <- ov$scores_by_subsector |> arrange( desc(gov_adj) )

sub |>
  transmute( Subsector = subsector, Organizations = num(n),
             `Mean score` = round(gov_mean, 2),
             `Size-adjusted` = round(gov_adj, 2),
             `Mean practices` = round(count_mean, 1) ) |>
  knitr::kable( align = "lrrrr" )
```

```{r, fig.height = 4.5}
sub_long <- bind_rows(
  data.frame( subsector = sub$subsector, value = sub$gov_mean, kind = "Raw mean" ),
  data.frame( subsector = sub$subsector, value = sub$gov_adj,  kind = "Size-adjusted" )
)
sub_long$subsector <- factor( sub_long$subsector, levels = rev(sub$subsector) )

ggplot( sub_long, aes(x = value, y = subsector, colour = kind, shape = kind) ) +
  geom_vline( xintercept = 0, colour = "grey70" ) +
  geom_point( size = 3 ) +
  scale_colour_manual( values = c(`Raw mean` = "#a2d4ec", `Size-adjusted` = blue),
                       name = NULL ) +
  scale_shape_manual( values = c(`Raw mean` = 1, `Size-adjusted` = 16), name = NULL ) +
  labs( x = "Mean gov_score", y = NULL ) +
  theme( legend.position = "top" )
```

Much of the raw difference between subsectors is size. Hospitals and
universities have the highest raw means (about 0.8 and 0.7) because they are
large; compared with organizations of the same size they are only slightly
above average. After adjusting for size, public and societal benefit and
health organizations score highest, and religion-related organizations score
lowest by a wide margin (a quarter of a point below organizations of the same
size). Read the "Unclassified" row with care: about one in six filers has no
usable NTEE code in the Business Master File.

## Geography

Size-adjusted state means span about half a point, from New Hampshire and the
District of Columbia at the top to Utah and North Dakota at the bottom: much less
than the size gradient, and similar to the spread across subsectors. The table
lists the five highest and lowest states; the chart shows every state.

```{r}
st <- ov$scores_by_state |> arrange( desc(gov_adj) )

st_tab <- st |>
  transmute( State = state, Organizations = num(n),
             `Mean score` = round(gov_mean, 2),
             `Size-adjusted` = round(gov_adj, 2) )

knitr::kable( rbind(head(st_tab, 5), tail(st_tab, 5)), row.names = FALSE,
              align = "lrrr" )
```

```{r, fig.height = 8}
st$state <- factor( st$state, levels = rev(st$state) )

ggplot( st, aes(x = gov_adj, y = state) ) +
  geom_vline( xintercept = 0, colour = "grey70" ) +
  geom_segment( aes(x = 0, xend = gov_adj, yend = state), colour = "#a2d4ec" ) +
  geom_point( colour = blue, size = 2 ) +
  labs( x = "Size-adjusted mean gov_score", y = NULL ) +
  theme( axis.text.y = element_text(size = 7) )
```

State differences may reflect charity regulation: some states require audits
or reviews above revenue thresholds, and some require registered charities to
adopt particular policies. The index does not separate those rules from other
regional differences.

## Organization age

Older organizations report more practices, and the gradient remains, smaller,
after adjusting for size: organizations under five years old score about a tenth
of a point below others of their size, and those over 40 years old about a tenth
above. Age is years since the IRS ruling date (or, where missing, the year of
formation on the 990).

```{r}
ov$scores_by_age |>
  transmute( Age = age_band, Organizations = num(n),
             `Mean score` = round(gov_mean, 2),
             `Size-adjusted` = round(gov_adj, 2),
             `Mean practices` = round(count_mean, 1) ) |>
  knitr::kable( align = "lrrrr" )
```

## Specific factors

The four specific-factor scores show where groups depart from what their
general score predicts. They average zero by construction, so they are most
useful for comparing groups. Larger organizations do *more* financial assurance
and have more pay-setting processes than their general score predicts, which
echoes the size effect on audits discussed in `vignette("making-gov-scores")`.
Minutes and written policies show no size pattern beyond the general score.
The written-policies factor has almost no variance of its own and should not be
used as a subscore. It appears here only for completeness (see
`vignette("governance-workflow")`).

```{r}
sz |>
  transmute( Size = size,
             `Financial assurance` = round(finance, 2),
             Minutes = round(minutes, 2),
             `Written policies` = round(policy, 2),
             Compensation = round(comp, 2) ) |>
  knitr::kable( align = "lrrrr" )
```

## Risk disclosures

Risk events are reported separately from the index. Insider business
transactions rise steeply with size, from 1% of the smallest organizations to
23% of the largest, and management companies rise from 3% to 7%. That is the
opposite of what a "bad governance" reading would predict: larger organizations
have more transactions to disclose and more processes for finding them. Loans
to insiders and family or business ties among officers are roughly flat across
sizes.

```{r}
rb <- ov$items_by_size
rb <- rb[ grepl("^RISK_", rb$item), ]
rb$label <- item_labels[ as.character(rb$item) ]

rb |>
  mutate( rate = pct(rate) ) |>
  select( label, size, rate ) |>
  tidyr::pivot_wider( names_from = size, values_from = rate ) |>
  rename( Disclosure = label ) |>
  knitr::kable()
```

Asset diversions are reported by about 1 in 1,000 filers, too few to analyze
here.

## Change over time, 2021--2024

Because the item parameters are fixed at 2023 values, scores from different
years are directly comparable. Across the whole population, the mean score
*fell* slightly from 2021 to 2024, and so did the mean number of practices.

```{r}
ov$population |>
  transmute( `Tax year` = year, Organizations = num(n),
             `Mean score` = round(gov_mean, 3),
             SD = round(gov_sd, 2),
             `Mean practices` = round(count_mean, 2) ) |>
  knitr::kable( align = "lrrrr" )
```

```{r, fig.height = 5}
iy <- ov$items_by_year
iy <- iy[ grepl("^GI_", iy$item), ]

iy_change <- iy |>
  group_by( item ) |>
  summarise( r2021 = rate[ year == 2021 ], r2024 = rate[ year == 2024 ] ) |>
  mutate( label = item_labels[ as.character(item) ] )

ggplot( iy_change, aes(y = reorder(label, r2024)) ) +
  geom_segment( aes(x = r2021, xend = r2024, yend = reorder(label, r2024)),
                colour = "#a2d4ec", linewidth = 1.2 ) +
  geom_point( aes(x = r2021), colour = "#a2d4ec", size = 2.5 ) +
  geom_point( aes(x = r2024), colour = blue, size = 2.5 ) +
  scale_x_continuous( labels = scales::percent ) +
  labs( x = "Share reporting the practice: 2021 (light) and 2024 (dark)",
        y = NULL )
```

Most practices were flat. The exceptions are the financial-assurance items:
the share of filers reporting an audit, an audit committee, or a review or
audit each fell by three to four points, and accrual accounting by about two.
Population means mix two things, though: change within organizations, and
organizations entering or leaving the full-990 population. The table below follows the
`r num(ov$change_overall$n)` organizations that filed a full 990 in both 2021
and 2024.

```{r}
co <- ov$change_overall
```

Among them, `r pct(co$share_up)` reported more practices in 2024 than in 2021,
`r pct(co$share_same)` the same number and `r pct(co$share_down)` fewer, and
the mean score rose by `r sprintf("%.2f", co$d_gov)`. Continuing organizations
improved, so the falling population mean points to composition: the
organizations entering the full-990 population report fewer practices than
those leaving it. One possible reason: the thresholds for filing the 990-EZ
instead are fixed in dollars, so inflation moves more small organizations onto
the full 990 each year, and small organizations are less often audited. Gains were largest in the middle size
bands; the largest organizations, already near the ceiling, barely changed.

```{r}
ov$change_by_size |>
  transmute( `Size (2023)` = size, Organizations = num(n),
             `Mean 2021` = round(gov_2021, 2), `Mean 2024` = round(gov_2024, 2),
             Change = sprintf("%+.3f", d_gov),
             `More practices` = pct(share_up),
             `Same` = pct(share_same),
             `Fewer` = pct(share_down) ) |>
  knitr::kable( align = "lrrrrrrr" )
```

Year-to-year changes in a single organization's count are common in both
directions, and many are one practice, so individual changes are noisy.
Changes in the average are more reliable than changes for any one
organization.

## Caveats

* **Reported, not observed.** The 990 records whether a policy exists, not
  whether it is followed.
* **Full 990 filers only.** Smaller organizations that file the 990-EZ or 990-N
  are not covered; their governance is likely weaker than the smallest band
  here.
* **Size and audits.** Audit, review and accrual items function differently by
  size (see `vignette("making-gov-scores")`). Size-adjusted comparisons reduce,
  but do not remove, that effect.
* **Descriptive only.** None of the differences above are causal.

## Producing your own breakouts

The same tables can be built for any sample: score it, join size, sector or
place from the Business Master File, and summarise by group. For example, with
a scored data frame `scores` that has an `expenses` column:

```{r, echo = TRUE, eval = FALSE}
breaks <- c( -Inf, 1e5, 5e5, 2e6, 1e7, 4e7, Inf )
labels <- c( "<$100k", "$100k-500k", "$500k-2m", "$2m-10m", "$10m-40m", "$40m+" )

scores$size <- cut( scores$expenses, breaks, labels, right = FALSE )

scores |>
  group_by( size ) |>
  summarise( n = n(), mean_score = mean(gov_score, na.rm = TRUE),
             audited = mean(GI_AUDIT, na.rm = TRUE) )
```
